brief.headline: Carlota has new evening confusion (including leaving the stove on), a 6% weight loss over about 12 weeks, and a decline in bathing and dressing independence, all after a Nov 2 ED visit for chest pain.

items.statement: On 2026-11-25 the RN noted about two weeks of increased evening confusion, with the stove left on once. She was oriented to person and place but not date, and had no fever. The plan was urinalysis, medication review, and a PCP visit this week.
items.verifier_note: Every detail matches the 2026-11-25 RN note.

items.statement: Weight fell from 73.5 kg on 2026-09-05 to 69.0 kg on 2026-11-24 (-4.5 kg, -6.1%), with a steady decline across all four readings. On 11-24 the dietitian noted poor appetite, skipped breakfasts, and about 50% of day center lunches eaten. Plan: oral supplement twice daily, weekly weights, and a dental check for chewing problems.
items.verifier_note: The vitals record has four readings that decline steadily, with a change of -4.5 kg (-6.1%). The dietitian note supports the appetite, breakfast, 50% lunch and plan details.

items.statement: On 2026-10-04 OT found she now needs moderate assistance with bathing and lower-body dressing; she was independent at the last review. OT recommended a tub transfer bench, a handheld shower, and more home care hours for bathing.
items.verifier_note: The OT note matches on the assistance levels, the prior independence and all three recommendations.

items.statement: On 2026-09-30 the home care aide gave hands-on help getting her out of the tub. Carlota said she has been skipping showers because she fears slipping. No fall is documented in these notes.
items.verifier_note: The aide note supports the hands-on help and the fear of slipping. The note mentions no fall, so the absence statement holds for the cited notes.

items.statement: She went to the partner hospital ED on 2026-11-02 for chest pain. The cardiac workup was negative, and she was released the same day with no new medications. On 11-07 the PCP found her back to baseline per her son and planned close monitoring for two weeks.
items.verifier_note: The ED summary, the encounter record and the PCP follow-up note support every detail.

items.statement: The medication record shows no starts or stops since 2026-09-01. Naproxen sodium (since 2003) is still active alongside clopidogrel, and the RN has planned a medication review for the new confusion.
items.verifier_note: The medication record shows no starts or stops, and the RN note shows a planned medication review. The cited sources contain no medication list, so they do not show naproxen sodium (since 2003) or clopidogrel as active.

questions_for_team: Could the new evening confusion be linked to the weight loss, reduced intake, or her medications? What do the urinalysis and medication review show?
Has the OT's bathing equipment and home care hours increase been put in place, and is she bathing safely?
Is the stove safety risk (left on once) covered at home, and what is the plan for evening supervision?
Who is following up the weight loss plan (supplements, weekly weights, dental check), and what is the trigger for escalation?
Should naproxen be reviewed given she is on clopidogrel and has ischemic heart disease?

checks: Confirm the review window (2026-09-01 to 2026-11-30) and pull all encounters in it: ED visits, urgent care, hospital admissions, observation stays, and any readmissions, with reasons and discharge instructions.

Cardiac events: chest pain or angina episodes, use of nitroglycerin spray (frequency and circumstances), syncope, palpitations, dyspnea, and any cardiology visits or testing since the ischemic heart disease onset (2025-10-06). Review whether the metoprolol, clopidogrel, simvastatin and nitroglycerin regimen is still active and documented as reviewed.

Bleeding and antiplatelet safety: because clopidogrel is active alongside naproxen (NSAID started 2003), check for any GI bleeding signs (melena, hematemesis, anemia on recent labs), bruising, epistaxis, or new GI complaints. Flag the naproxen plus clopidogrel combination for prescriber review without recommending a change.

Medication reconciliation: list all starts and stops in the window, check for duplicate or missing prescriptions, confirm pharmacy fill history and adherence for the five active medications, and note any OTC analgesic use beyond naproxen.

Blood pressure and heart rate trend: review recorded BP and HR at each contact in the window, especially orthostatic readings and any low readings on metoprolol, and note any dizziness or falls associated with them.

Falls and mobility: check for any falls, near-falls, or fall-related injuries, given hip osteoarthritis, chronic low back pain, fibromyalgia and possible antiplatelet therapy. Review gait, transfers, assistive device use, and whether PT or fall-risk screening is due.

Pain management: review pain scores, pain interference with function and sleep, and any change in analgesic use, including naproxen dose and frequency. Check whether pain control plans are documented and due for review.

Weight and nutrition: obtain weight trend since last review (obesity, BMI 30+), appetite, dietary changes, and any cardiometabolic monitoring such as glucose or lipid labs with simvastatin on record. Note whether a dietitian or weight-related referral is due.

Dental and sinus follow-up: check for dental visits, reports of pain, chewing difficulty or intake impact related to loss of teeth, and chronic sinusitis symptoms, treatments, or ENT contact in the window.

Function, cognition, mood, and social: review ADL and IADL changes, cognitive screening results if due, mood screening (PHQ or similar), social engagement, and attendance at PACE day center or programs. Confirm caregiver or family situation and any caregiver strain, and check that all care-plan items due in the window (assessments, reviews, goals, IDT referrals) are completed or scheduled before 2026-11-30.
